This men's blanket-lined denim jacket is made in Vietnam for Lee's Japanese-market collection and developed by EDWIN under license from The H.D. Lee Company, Inc., U.S.A. Its design draws on the lineage of Lee's 101-J Riders Jacket, the blanket-lined 101-LJ, and the later Storm Rider, bringing the recognizable construction and cold-weather character of these classic American denim jackets into a contemporary casual model.

The jacket combines a one-washed 13 oz cotton indigo denim shell with a brushed, striped wool-blend blanket lining through the body and sleeves and a contrasting brown corduroy point collar. A six-button front, zigzag-stitched folded plackets, angled chest pockets with curved buttoned flaps, sewn front darts, set-in sleeves with single-button cuffs, a multi-panel back, and buttoned waistband adjusters retain the characteristic details of the Riders Jacket design. Lee Workwear Heritage and the 101-J Riders Jacket
Lee was founded in Kansas, USA, in 1889 and has grown into one of America's best-known jeans and workwear brands. After its founding, the company began producing practical garments such as overalls, UNION-ALLS, and work jackets, and later developed numerous models closely associated with the history of American workwear and denim, including cowboy clothing, Lee COWBOY, the 101 series, RIDERS, the 101-J, 101-LJ, STORM RIDER, and WESTERNER. Today, Lee continues to produce denim-centered casual wear while incorporating functional details and construction rooted in traditional workwear.

The LM5110 is a men's blanket-lined denim jacket that carries forward the heritage of the STORM RIDER, one of Lee's signature insulated denim jackets. It combines a 13 oz indigo denim outer shell with a striped wool-blend blanket lining and a brown-toned corduroy collar, increasing insulation and warmth. The jacket is developed by EDWIN Co., Ltd., which operates the Lee brand in Japan, under license from The H.D. Lee Company, Inc., U.S.A., and is manufactured in Vietnam.

The design foundation of the LM5110 is Lee's iconic 101-J RIDERS JACKET. Developed from the earlier Lee COWBOY JACKET lineage, the 101-J became established as a distinctive denim jacket characterized by diagonally positioned chest pockets, two-line front darts, a short body length, and set-in sleeves.

From the Blanket-Lined 101-LJ to the Storm Rider
Based on the 101-J design, the blanket-lined 101-LJ appeared in the late 1940s as a version with increased cold-weather protection. While retaining the basic front design and body construction of the 101-J, the 101-LJ added an insulating blanket lining and adopted a corduroy collar in place of the denim collar, resulting in a warmer construction with greater insulation.

The 101-LJ was later offered under the STORM RIDER name, and the combination of a corduroy collar and striped blanket lining became established as one of Lee's characteristic insulated denim-jacket designs.

Contemporary Interpretation with a Secured Lining Hem
The LM5110 is not a vintage reproduction intended to faithfully duplicate every specification of a particular production year of the 101-LJ or STORM RIDER. Instead, it incorporates characteristic design and construction elements carried forward from the 101-J through the 101-LJ and STORM RIDER, reworked into a denim jacket suited to contemporary wear.

Certain early-1950s 101-LJ jackets used a free-hanging blanket-lining construction in which the lower edge of the lining was not sewn into the waistband, allowing some movement at the bottom of the lining. In contrast, the LM5110 secures the lower edge of the blanket lining into the waistband construction. Inside the collar, the jacket also features a label with the STORM RIDER name and artwork depicting a cowboy and a snowy landscape. Rather than reproducing an early 101-LJ exactly, the LM5110 incorporates features carried forward through the 101-LJ and later STORM RIDER while adapting them to a contemporary construction.

13 oz 100% Cotton Deep Indigo Denim Shell
The outer shell is made from 13 oz, 100% cotton deep indigo denim. The fabric retains a moderate degree of body and firmness while also offering a supple feel.

One-Wash Finish and Subsequent Shrinkage
A one-wash treatment is applied during the finishing process. This treatment eases some of the denim's initial stiffness, giving the fabric a more accommodating feel from the beginning compared with unwashed denim.

The initial wash also allows part of the fabric's early shrinkage to occur before sale, helping reduce the larger dimensional change normally associated with the first wash of an untreated garment. Some additional shrinkage may still occur depending on washing method, drying conditions, and repeated laundering.

Indigo Fading and Wear at Folds and Seams
With continued wear and washing, the denim gradually settles and develops variations in its indigo coloration. Areas exposed to frequent movement and friction, including the sleeve bends, front plackets, chest pocket areas, seams, cuffs, and hem, will gradually develop wear marks and lighter tones.

The fading and contrast that develop in the deep indigo denim, together with the changes that appear around the fabric and stitched areas, are characteristic of the garment's natural aging process.

Brushed Striped Recycled-Wool-Blend Blanket Lining
The body and sleeves are lined with a brushed striped blanket fabric made from a blend containing recycled wool. The lining combines multiple colored stripes and has the raised fibrous surface and irregular neps characteristic of a wool-blend blanket fabric.

The blanket lining helps create an insulating air layer inside the garment, increasing warmth and cold-weather protection.

Six-Button Front and Folded Plackets with Zigzag Stitching
The jacket has a full-opening front secured with six metal buttons. The front edges are turned inward to create a double-layer construction, reinforcing the plackets along the opening.

Lee's characteristic zigzag stitching is applied to the plackets. This stitching secures and stabilizes the doubled fabric while also creating one of the recognizable details associated with Lee RIDERS JACKET construction and classic Lee workwear. The buttonholes are positioned horizontally across the vertical front opening.

Brown Corduroy Point Collar without a Separate Collar Stand
The collar is made from brown-toned corduroy, creating a contrast in both texture and color against the denim body.

It has a classic point-collar shape and a standless construction, with no separate collar stand between the collar and neckline. The collar is attached directly to the neckline in a construction characteristic of traditional work jackets. Corduroy also provides a softer contact surface around the neck than denim, contributing to comfort where the collar comes into contact with the skin.

Angled Front Yokes and Rounded Chest Patch Pockets
The upper front is divided by yoke seams that rise diagonally from the center toward the sides, and the chest pockets are positioned in line with this angled construction.

Each chest pocket is an externally applied patch pocket with rounded lower corners and a curved flap shaped to complement the rounded form of the pocket body. A buttonhole is positioned at the center of each flap, allowing the flap to fasten over a button attached to the pocket body. A small Lee logo tab is sewn into the edge of the left chest pocket flap.

Sewn Front Darts for Body Shaping
Two-line front darts run from each chest pocket down to the upper edge of the waistband. These darts are formed by folding the body fabric inward and securing it with stitching.

The darts shape the front body three-dimensionally while emphasizing the vertical lines of the jacket and also serving as a visual design accent. They are not action pleats designed to open and provide additional range of motion; instead, they are a construction detail used to shape the front body.

Set-In Sleeve Construction
The sleeves use set-in construction and are attached to the body along defined shoulder seams.

Single-Button Cuffs with Sleeve Plackets
Each sleeve ends in a cuff with a single metal-button closure and a functional sleeve placket. When the button is released, the sleeve opening can spread wider, making the jacket easier to put on and take off.

Antiqued Lee RIDERS Metal Buttons
The metal buttons have an antiqued finish with a subdued brass-toned appearance. The face of each button is engraved with the "Lee RIDERS" name, adding a classic Lee workwear detail to the front closure, chest pockets, and cuffs.

Back Yoke and Multi-Panel Body Construction
The upper back is divided by a separate back yoke. Below the yoke, a large center-back panel is joined to side panels on the left and right, creating a multi-panel body construction.

The vertical panel seams help shape the back of the jacket and define its rear construction.

Rear Waistband Adjusters with Plastic Cat's-Eye Buttons
Adjustment tabs are positioned at the left and right sides of the rear waistband. One end of each tab is permanently sewn to the jacket, while the opposite end has a buttonhole and fastens to plastic cat's-eye buttons.

Under normal conditions, the tab is held at the outer button position. Moving it to the inner button position draws in the waistband, allowing the waist area to be tightened.

Storm Rider Label inside the Collar
Inside the collar, a brand label featuring the STORM RIDER name and graphic artwork is sewn into the jacket.

Made in Vietnam for Lee's Japanese-Market Collection
The jacket is developed by EDWIN Co., Ltd., which operates the Lee brand in Japan, under license from The H.D. Lee Company, Inc., U.S.A., and is manufactured in Vietnam.

The LM5110 is based on Lee's iconic 101-J RIDERS JACKET and incorporates characteristic elements developed through the blanket-lined 101-LJ and the later STORM RIDER, including the corduroy collar and blanket lining. These established Lee details are brought together in a contemporary model intended for everyday wear.

Care Instructions
- Machine wash on a gentle cycle at a maximum water temperature of 40°C / 104°F.
- Do not use chlorine bleach or oxygen bleach.
- Do not tumble dry.
- Hang to dry in the shade.
- Iron with a pressing cloth at a maximum soleplate temperature of 150°C / 302°F.
- Do not dry clean.
- Professional wet cleaning using a very gentle process is permitted.

The garment has been washed once during finishing. Some additional shrinkage may still occur depending on the washing method, drying conditions, and repeated laundering. Please always follow the care instructions attached to the actual product.

Due to the nature of indigo-dyed products, dye may transfer to other clothing, bags, furniture, or other surfaces through friction during wear or when the garment becomes damp from perspiration or rain. Please take particular care when wearing the jacket with white or light-colored clothing or using it near light-colored items.

Wash separately from other garments, as indigo dye may be released during laundering. To help prevent discoloration, do not use bleach or detergents containing bleaching agents. Prolonged exposure to sunlight or artificial lighting may also cause discoloration or fading, so please take care when storing the garment.

Important Notes
The Lee logo buttons used on this jacket are not installed with the logo aligned in a uniform direction. The orientation of the "Lee" lettering may therefore vary between button positions and individual garments. This is part of the product specification and is not a defect.

product.title: TOYS McCOY Men's Steve McQueen "The Great Escape" Reproduction Chino Pants, Military Trousers, 12.5 oz. Cotton Twill, Slim Straight Fit, Button Fly, Made in Japan (TMP2604, 040 Khaki)
product.body_html:
TOYS McCOY Men's Steve McQueen "The Great Escape" Reproduction Chino Pants, Military Trousers, 12.5 oz. Cotton Twill, Slim Straight Fit, Button Fly, Made in Japan (TMP2604, 040 Khaki)

TOYS McCOY

These men's khaki chino trousers are made in Japan by TOYS McCOY as a reproduction of the screen costume worn by Steve McQueen as Captain Virgil Hilts in The Great Escape. The design takes U.S. military chino trousers as its foundation while focusing specifically on the slimmer proportions, distinctive cut, and details of the trousers prepared for McQueen's appearance in the film. Unlike the roomier, utility-oriented silhouettes commonly associated with U.S. military chino trousers of the World War II era, the trousers seen on McQueen in the film are said to have been modified at his request for a cleaner, more streamlined appearance. For this reason, this model is not intended as a direct reproduction of a particular period-issued military specification. Instead, it recreates the screen costume itself, which was based on U.S. military chinos but altered to suit McQueen's preferred silhouette and the visual requirements of the film. TOYS McCOY has reconstructed these characteristics in a modern reproduction by considering the differences in silhouette from conventional military chinos, together with the texture and khaki tone of the fabric, button-fly front, pocket construction, and other period-inspired details. The flat front, mid rise, and slim straight legs combine the distinctive character of McQueen's screen-worn trousers with the practical construction of classic chino trousers, resulting in a style that remains highly wearable for contemporary casual use.

Size and Fit Guide:

Gender: Men.

Our model is wearing a tagged size 30. He is 5'9" (175 cm) tall, weighs approximately 130 lbs (59 kg), and has a chest measurement of approximately 36" (91 cm). His usual jeans size is 29.

Fit: These trousers have a slim straight fit, a standard mid rise, a flat front without pleats, and a button-fly closure. The seat and thighs have a more streamlined shape than traditional wide military chinos, while retaining room for everyday movement. The legs narrow very gently from the knees to the hems, maintaining a natural straight-leg appearance without a pronounced taper. The fabric has been one-washed to reduce initial shrinkage and ease its initial stiffness.

The actual waist measurements tend to run smaller than the tagged sizes suggest. If you prefer a little extra room at the waist, you may wish to consider one tagged size up as a starting point. Because the rise and waistband position affect how trousers fit, please measure a similar pair of chino pants that fits you well and compare the waist, front rise, thigh, and leg opening measurements before choosing your size.

Available sizes: 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 36, and 38.

Steve McQueen V. Hilts Screen-Costume Reproduction
These trousers reproduce the khaki pants worn by Steve McQueen in his role as Captain Virgil Hilts in The Great Escape. The costume trousers are said to have been altered at McQueen's request to create slimmer, cleaner proportions than the practical, wider silhouettes commonly associated with World War II U.S. military chinos.

The reproduction focuses on that modified screen costume rather than a single military-issued trouser pattern or a specific military specification. TOYS McCOY brings together the distinctive silhouette, closely woven fabric, subdued khaki color, button fly, pocket construction, and interior costume markings to reproduce the character of the trousers seen in the film.

Flat Front, Mid Rise, and Slim Straight Legs
The front is cut without pleats, keeping the fabric relatively flat across the upper front. A standard mid rise places the waistband neither unusually low nor especially high. The seat and thighs are shaped with less volume than traditional wide military chinos, creating a slimmer profile through the upper legs.

From the knees to the hems, the legs narrow only very gently. This slight reduction in width preserves a natural straight-leg line instead of producing a strongly tapered leg opening. The cut retains space for normal movement and is not intended to fit closely against the body like a skinny silhouette.

The resulting balance reflects the streamlined proportions of the film costume while retaining the practical ease of everyday trousers. The flat front and restrained leg shape allow the texture and color of the chino cloth to remain central to the overall appearance.

12.5 oz. 100% Cotton Chino Twill
The main fabric is 12.5 oz. chino cloth woven from 100% cotton. Its twill structure produces fine diagonal ribs across the surface. These closely spaced ribs are combined with a dense weave, giving the fabric a compact feel and a noticeable degree of body and resilience.

The cloth has enough firmness to support the shape of the trousers while remaining supple enough to bend with the wearer. This balance of structure and flexibility preserves the practical character of military-style chinos without making the fabric feel uniformly rigid.

The light, subdued khaki shade reflects the appearance of the movie costume. Fine twill definition and a closely woven surface give the fabric a clean appearance while retaining the substantial character of military trouser cloth. It is neither an extremely thin fabric nor a thick winter-specific cloth, making it suitable for casual wear across an extended portion of the year.

One-Wash Finish and Changes Through Wear
The trousers receive a one-wash treatment during finishing. Washing relaxes some of the initial stiffness of the densely woven chino cloth, making it easier to wear from the beginning while preserving the fabric's underlying body.

Because the garment has already been washed during production, the potential for substantial shrinkage after purchase is reduced compared with an unwashed garment. This does not mean the fabric is completely shrink-free. A small amount of further shrinkage may occur depending on the washing method and drying conditions.

With repeated wear and washing, the cotton fabric gradually becomes softer and more familiar to the wearer's movements. The fine twill surface also develops subtle changes in appearance as the cloth relaxes and is handled through everyday use.

Five-Button Fly with Four-Hole Urea Buttons
The front opening uses a traditional button fly comprising one top button at the waistband and four additional buttons inside the fly, for a total of five. The lower buttons are concealed within the fly construction when the trousers are fastened.

The buttons are made from urea resin and have four sewing holes. Their color coordinates with the khaki outer fabric, keeping the fastenings visually integrated with the trousers. The waistband button closes the top of the opening, while the four lower buttons secure the fly at successive points below it.

Separately Secured Buttonhole Sections
Below the top waistband buttonhole, the buttonhole side of the fly is secured with short stitches positioned between the individual buttonholes. These stitches divide the fly into separate sections, each containing one buttonhole.

This construction holds the fly layers together at intervals between the fastenings rather than leaving the entire buttonhole strip unsecured between its ends. The short securing stitches are a distinct construction detail within the concealed front opening.

Slanted Front Hand Pockets
The trousers have five pockets in total. Two hand pockets are positioned at the front, with their openings set at a diagonal on the left and right sides. The slanted entry follows a natural angle for inserting the hand.

The diagonal openings sit alongside the unpleated front, providing practical access without interrupting the overall flat-front arrangement. The pocket bags are contained inside the trousers.

Single-Welt Coin or Watch Pocket
A small horizontal pocket is set into the upper right front. Its opening is finished with a single welt, creating a narrow, defined edge at the entrance.

The compact pocket can be used for coins, a watch, or similarly small items. Its inset construction keeps the storage compartment inside the garment while presenting a discreet horizontal opening on the outside.

Single-Welt Inset Back Pockets
Two back pockets are positioned horizontally, one on each side of the rear. Each opening uses a single-welt construction, giving the pocket entrance a narrow, clearly defined finish.

The pocket bags are housed inside the trousers. Unlike an external patch pocket, this inset arrangement leaves only the welt and opening visible on the outside, maintaining a clean rear surface while providing accessible storage.

Off-White Cotton Drill Pocket Bags and Waistband Reinforcement
The front and rear pocket bags are made from off-white cotton drill with a tone close to natural ecru. Drill is a sturdy woven cotton fabric with a diagonal twill structure, making it a practical material for pocket interiors that repeatedly come into contact with hands and stored items.

The same off-white drill is used as reinforcement on the inside of the waistband. This additional fabric supports the inner waistband construction and creates a consistent interior finish alongside the pocket bags. Its lighter shade also distinguishes these internal components from the khaki outer cloth.

Interior Size Stamp and Costume Name Label
The inside of the waistband carries a size stamp and a costume name label. The label includes the wording "Toys McCoy Costume Co. Hollywood," Steve McQueen's name, and spaces for waist and inseam information.

These markings reproduce the name and sizing details associated with McQueen's trousers. Although hidden during normal wear, they reinforce the garment's identity as a reproduction of a film costume and extend that reference into the interior construction.

The entries "WAIST 32" and "INSEAM 31" are reproduced costume details associated with Steve McQueen's pants size. They are not the size designation or actual measurements of this garment. Please use the product's tagged size and the actual measurement charts when selecting your size.

Seven Belt Loops with an Offset Rear Loop
Seven relatively narrow belt loops are attached around the waistband. Their slim proportions keep the loops visually restrained while allowing a belt to be supported at multiple positions around the waist.

The loop near the center back is placed slightly to the left of the rear center seam. The rear seam and its allowances already create an area of overlapping fabric. Moving the loop away from that point is understood to avoid adding the loop's thickness directly over the existing layers, reflecting a practical approach to managing bulk during construction.

Tonal Stitching and Reinforced Attachment Points
The sewing thread is predominantly tonal, blending with the khaki fabric. Stitching around the pocket openings, fly, waistband, and belt loops defines these components without creating excessive contrast against the main cloth.

Reinforcement stitches are used at points that receive concentrated stress during wear and movement, including the ends of pocket openings and the attachment points of belt loops. These additional stitches support the areas where repeated pulling and handling place greater demands on the sewn construction.

Overlocked Inseam Allowances
Inside the legs, the edges of the inseam allowances are finished with overlock stitching. The stitches wrap around the exposed fabric edges to help contain the cut yarns and limit fraying.

This is an internal edge finish at the inseam. It keeps the seam allowances more securely contained in an area repeatedly exposed to movement and contact during wear.

Deep Turned Hems with Single-Row Stitching
At each leg opening, the main fabric is turned inward by a relatively generous amount and secured with a single row of stitching. The fold forms the finished lower edge, while the turned fabric remains inside the leg.

This construction adds a layer of the same chino cloth at the opening. The single row of stitching secures the turned portion to the leg while keeping the visible hem finish simple.

Made in Japan
These trousers are made in Japan as part of TOYS McCOY's reproduction of Steve McQueen's V. Hilts wardrobe. McQueen's screen clothing was shaped through adjustments to details such as shirt and jacket sleeve lengths and the width and balance of trousers, helping the costume suit both the character's movements and his appearance on screen.

This model brings that approach together through its slim straight silhouette, dense khaki chino twill, button fly, slanted front pockets, single-welt rear pockets, off-white interior components, and costume name label. The combination preserves the specific character of the film wardrobe within a practical pair of cotton chino trousers.

Care Instructions
Hand wash.
Do not use chlorine bleach or oxygen bleach.
Iron at a maximum soleplate temperature of 110°C (230°F), with a pressing cloth between the iron and the garment.
Do not dry clean.
Drip dry in the shade without spin-drying.
Do not tumble dry.
Although the trousers have been one-washed, slight additional shrinkage may occur depending on washing and drying conditions.
Always follow the care instructions attached to the actual product.

product.body_html:
Buzz Rickson's Men's Type WEP Flight Jacket MIL-S-18342C U.S. Navy Reproduction BR15947 Olive

Buzz Rickson

This men's Type WEP flight jacket is made in Japan by Buzz Rickson's, Toyo Enterprises' military label specializing in reproductions and interpretations of vintage American military clothing. The jacket reproduces the later U.S. Navy WEP winter flying-suit configuration made to the MIL-S-18342C specification, commonly referred to as the C-Type and associated with the 1972 model. Its construction combines an Olive plain-weave nylon shell, a full cotton-canvas lining, a nylon-and-polyester pile interlining, a wool rib-knit collar and cuffs, distinctive V-shaped cuff-to-sleeve junctions, an action back for increased shoulder mobility, a SCOVILL-marked brass zipper with a horsehide pull tab, an internal wind flap, large flap-covered front patch pockets, a left upper-sleeve utility pocket, and a gathered fabric-covered waistband. Four internal attachment tabs reflect the jacket's original role as the upper component of a two-piece winter flying suit designed to connect with matching trousers. The pile interlining adds insulation, thickness, and volume through the body and sleeves, while the gathered waist and tapered knit cuffs help create the rounded silhouette characteristic of the later WEP design.

Size and Fit Guide:

Gender: Men.

The jacket has a classic flight-jacket fit, with generous room through the body and sleeves combined with a comparatively short body length. Rather than using an excessively broad shoulder width, it creates volume through its roomy chest, full armholes and upper sleeves, compact length, and gathered waistband, which draws the hem inward around the waist. Together, these elements give the upper body a rounded, three-dimensional silhouette characteristic of traditional flight jackets.

The jacket has an insulating layer between the shell and lining, giving the body and sleeves noticeably more thickness and structure than lightweight-zone flight jackets such as L-2 styles, which do not use comparable insulation. At the same time, the insulation occupies some of the internal wearing space, so although the jacket appears full and voluminous from the outside, the actual fit is not excessively loose.

Actual fit will vary depending on body type, the thickness of the layers worn underneath, and personal fit preference. When selecting your size, we recommend comparing the garment measurements listed below with those of a similar flight jacket that fits you well.

Type WEP MIL-S-18342C U.S. Navy Winter Flying Suit Jacket
This Type WEP flight jacket is produced by Buzz Rickson's, Toyo Enterprises' military label specializing in detailed reproductions and interpretations of historic American military garments. This model reproduces the later WEP configuration associated with the MIL-S-18342C specification and the 1972 model.

The WEP was developed as the jacket component of a two-piece U.S. Navy winter flying suit used in conjunction with corresponding trousers. Unlike a conventional stand-alone jacket, the original system was conceived so that the upper and lower garments could be physically connected. This relationship is preserved on the reproduction through attachment tabs installed inside the lower body of the jacket.

The WEP evolved through successive specification revisions, with MIL-S-18342C representing the final C-Type configuration. BR15947 incorporates a number of details associated with this later form, including its olive-colored nylon shell, insulated construction, distinctive V-shaped knit cuff junctions, bi-swing action back, fabric-covered elasticized waistband, large front pockets, upper-sleeve utility pocket, and internal trouser-attachment system.

100% Nylon Plain-Weave Outer Shell
The outer shell is made from 100% nylon woven in a plain-weave construction. In plain weave, the lengthwise warp yarns and crosswise weft yarns pass alternately over and under one another, creating a compact and evenly interlaced textile structure without the diagonal ribs of a twill weave or the reinforcement grid of ripstop fabric.

The resulting surface is fine, dense, and relatively smooth. Rather than having the hard, board-like hand sometimes associated with more rigid nylon fabrics, this shell has a softer and more pliable character that allows it to flex naturally with the movement of the garment.

The nylon does not have a bright or highly reflective finish. Instead, the surface shows a subdued, matte luster that changes subtly according to the direction of the light and viewing angle. Fine natural wrinkles in the fabric, together with light puckering around stitched areas, add dimensional variation to the otherwise smooth woven surface.

Earlier WEP configurations are associated with a comparatively lighter Leaf Green appearance, while the later C-Type is characterized by a stronger olive-green tone. This deeper olive coloration is one of the visual elements that distinguishes the later WEP configuration reproduced by this jacket.

Full 100% Cotton Canvas Lining
The interior is fully lined from the body through the sleeves with 100% cotton canvas. Although described as canvas, the lining has a comparatively soft and smooth surface rather than the exceptionally stiff or coarse hand associated with very heavy utility canvas.

The lining forms a continuous textile layer between the wearer's clothing and the enclosed insulating material. Its relatively smooth surface helps reduce friction against shirts, sweaters, and other layers worn underneath, allowing the jacket to slide more easily over the body during dressing and removal and reducing resistance when the arms move inside the sleeves.

In addition to providing the finished interior surface of the jacket, the cotton lining also serves as the mounting surface for internal components such as the identification label and trouser-attachment tabs.

70% Nylon / 30% Polyester Pile Insulation
Between the nylon outer shell and cotton lining is an insulating pile layer composed of 70% nylon and 30% polyester. The pile construction creates numerous small air spaces within the thickness of the material. These trapped pockets of air form an insulating layer that helps reduce the loss of body heat through the garment.

Unlike a thin shell jacket in which the outer fabric and lining lie relatively close together, the pile insulation adds measurable thickness between the two layers. This produces additional loft and structural volume through both the torso and sleeves.

The insulation therefore affects not only thermal performance but also the physical shape of the jacket. It gives the body and sleeves a fuller, more dimensional form and contributes directly to the rounded, substantial silhouette associated with the WEP flight-jacket design.

Long Set-In Sleeve Construction
The jacket uses conventional set-in sleeves. Each shaped sleeve is sewn into a defined armhole in the body, establishing a clear structural division between the shoulder section and sleeve rather than extending diagonally toward the neckline as in raglan construction.

Because the sleeves contain the same insulated layered construction as the body, they retain three-dimensional volume from the shoulder through the upper arm and forearm. The sleeve gradually narrows toward the rib-knit cuff, allowing the fuller insulated upper section to transition into a more closely fitted wrist opening.

SCOVILL-Marked Brass Front Zipper with Horsehide Pull Tab
The front opening is secured by a metal zipper using brass hardware. The zipper slider carries the "SCOVILL" marking, reproducing the utilitarian metal-fastener character associated with military flight garments.

A horsehide leather extension tab is attached to the metal zipper pull. By increasing the amount of material available to grasp, the leather tab provides a larger and more tactile operating surface than the metal pull alone. This makes the zipper easier to locate and manipulate, particularly when dexterity is reduced by gloves or cold-weather clothing.

The horsehide tab also separates the user's fingers from direct contact with the relatively small metal pull while preserving the straightforward mechanical construction of the front closure.

Full-Length Interior Wind Flap
A separate wind flap is positioned vertically behind the front zipper and extends along the opening. This additional layer sits directly behind the zipper elements, where small gaps would otherwise provide a relatively direct path for outside air to enter the interior of the jacket.

By placing another textile barrier behind the zipper, the construction helps reduce direct airflow through the center-front opening and limits cold air penetration into the garment. The flap also separates the metal zipper assembly from clothing worn underneath.

Multiple parallel rows of longitudinal stitching run along the wind flap. These stitch lines stabilize the layered construction, control shifting between the joined materials, and help the flap retain its narrow, elongated shape along the zipper opening.

100% Wool Rib-Knit Collar with Buttoned Throat Strap
The collar is made from 100% wool rib knit. Compared with the woven nylon body panels, the knitted structure provides greater flexibility and elasticity, allowing the collar to be worn folded down or raised around the neck.

A separate throat strap is attached to the left side of the collar. One end of the strap is permanently sewn to the collar, while a worked buttonhole is formed at the opposite end. A corresponding button is positioned on the right collar.

When the collar is raised, the strap can be extended across the front of the neck and secured to the button on the opposite side. This holds the collar in a stand-collar position and closes the open area around the throat more effectively, thereby increasing protection against direct airflow at the neckline.

When the throat strap is not being used, it can be secured to a retaining button on the left collar. This keeps the loose strap controlled against the collar instead of allowing it to hang freely.

100% Wool V-Shaped Rib-Knit Cuffs
The sleeve cuffs are also made from 100% wool rib knit. Unlike a conventional rib-knit cuff attached to the sleeve as a relatively straight band around the wrist, this construction incorporates a tapered extension of knit that projects upward into the lower sleeve.

As the knit section narrows toward the upper sleeve, its junction with the surrounding nylon shell forms a long V-shaped outline. The V therefore occurs at the interface between the woven sleeve and knitted cuff rather than as an open slit at the wrist edge.

This arrangement is intended to reduce excessive bulk where the insulated sleeve transitions into the wrist. Instead of carrying the full thickness of the padded woven sleeve directly to the cuff opening, part of the lower sleeve area is replaced by more flexible knitted material.

The construction allows the full, insulated sleeve to taper more naturally toward the wrist while the rib knit conforms more closely around the wearer's arm. This distinctive V-shaped cuff treatment is one of the recognizable construction details associated with the later C-Type WEP configuration.

Bi-Swing Action Back for Shoulder Mobility
Action pleats, also known as a bi-swing back, are incorporated at both sides of the rear body near the back armholes. The construction places additional fabric inside folded sections that remain relatively flat when the arms are in a neutral position.

When the wearer reaches forward, the folds can open and release this concealed fabric, temporarily increasing the effective width across the upper back and rear shoulder area. When less extension is required, the additional material returns into the folded structure.

This allows the jacket to maintain a comparatively compact body length while still providing additional room for forward arm movement. The system is particularly useful in a flight-jacket design, where freedom of movement through the shoulders and upper back must coexist with a short, controlled body silhouette.

Fabric-Covered Elasticized Gathered Waistband
The lower edge of the jacket does not use the exposed rib-knit waistband commonly seen on designs such as the MA-1. Instead, the WEP uses an elasticized waistband covered with fabric matching the general character of the outer shell.

Multiple horizontal rows of stitching run through the waistband, visually dividing it into narrow channels while stabilizing the gathered construction. The elasticized structure draws the comparatively roomy lower body inward around the waist.

This reduces the open circumference at the hem, controls excess volume through the lower torso, and helps keep the jacket closer to the body around the waist. Combined with the broad insulated body and sleeves, the gathered waistband contributes substantially to the characteristic rounded WEP silhouette, with volume concentrated through the upper body and controlled at the lower edge.

Gusseted Front Patch Pockets with Concealed Snap Closures
Large patch pockets are positioned on both front body panels. Each pocket is covered by a broad flap whose lower edges angle downward from both sides and meet at a central downward-facing point.

The flaps are secured by concealed snap fasteners. Because the snaps are hidden beneath the flaps, the exterior surfaces remain visually clean while the pockets can still be positively closed.

The upper edge of each pocket body is constructed so that it folds inward as the flap is opened and closed. This allows the pocket opening to move with the flap rather than remaining as a completely rigid horizontal edge.

Additional fabric is incorporated along the lower and outer portions of the pocket body to form gussets. These gusseted sections allow the pocket to expand outward when contents are inserted, giving it greater usable internal volume than a completely flat patch pocket while allowing it to lie closer to the jacket when lightly loaded.

On the wearer's left front pocket, a small buttonhole-shaped opening is positioned near the inner edge toward the front zipper. This opening is intended to accept a pen, providing a narrow dedicated access point separate from the primary pocket opening.

Left Upper-Sleeve Utility Pocket with Raw-Cut Flap Interior
A vertically oriented utility pocket is sewn onto the outside of the left upper sleeve. The pocket is covered by a rectangular flap and secured by a concealed snap fastener positioned beneath the flap.

This placement provides an additional storage compartment on the upper arm without interrupting the large front body pockets. The concealed fastening maintains the simple exterior profile of the flap while keeping the pocket opening secured.

The underside of the sleeve-pocket flap intentionally retains a raw-cut fabric edge rather than using a fully turned and clean-finished edge treatment. This simplified construction reflects the direct, utilitarian sewing methods associated with military garments, where functional assembly and efficient material use take priority over decorative interior finishing.

Four Interior Trouser-Attachment Tabs
Four short woven tape tabs are installed around the lower interior of the jacket. Each tab incorporates a worked buttonhole so that it can engage with the corresponding fastening points on the matching trousers.

These tabs are a direct reminder that the WEP was originally conceived as the upper half of a two-piece winter flying suit rather than solely as an independent outer jacket. Connecting the upper and lower garments helps maintain their relationship during movement and prevents the jacket and trousers from separating as freely as completely independent pieces.

A separate short woven tape loop is also positioned at the lower end of the internal wind flap. This component is distinct from the four buttonhole-equipped trouser-attachment tabs.

This product is sold as the jacket only. Matching trousers are not included.

Reproduction Military-Style Identification Label and Hanger Loop
A reproduction identification label is sewn inside the back neck area. Its layout and typography follow the general format associated with period military garment labels and reproduce a series of specification, identification, and procurement-style markings.

The visible wording includes "JACKET - SUITS, FLYING, WINTER," "MIL-S-18342 C (WEP)," "8415-286-7970," "BUZZ RICKSON MFG. CO., INC.," and "DSA 100-72-C-1243."

These markings reproduce the visual language of military garment identification, including the item designation, specification reference, stock-number-style identifier, manufacturer-style name, and contract-style number. The label therefore functions not merely as modern branding but also as part of the historical presentation of the reproduction.

A separate hanger loop is installed directly above the label, providing a convenient point from which the jacket can be hung without placing the full weight of the garment on the collar itself.

Later MIL-S-18342C Type WEP Configuration
BR15947 combines the principal construction elements associated with the later Type WEP configuration: a plain-weave nylon outer shell, full cotton-canvas lining, nylon-and-polyester pile insulation, wool rib-knit collar and V-shaped cuffs, SCOVILL-marked brass zipper, internal wind flap, bi-swing action back, fabric-covered gathered waistband, gusseted front pockets, left upper-sleeve utility pocket, and internal trouser-attachment system.

Together, these components reproduce the layered, insulated, and equipment-oriented character of the MIL-S-18342C-period WEP while preserving the compact body length, substantial sleeve volume, controlled waist, and rounded profile that distinguish this U.S. Navy flight-jacket design.

Model
Buzz Rickson's by Toyo Enterprises / Lot No. BR15947 / Type WEP "BUZZ RICKSON MFG. CO., INC."


Care Instructions
Do not wash.
Do not bleach.
Do not tumble dry.
Do not iron.
Do not dry clean.
Do not professionally wet clean.
For cleaning and maintenance, please consult a professional cleaner experienced with specialized outerwear and military-style garments.

Special Care for Buzz Rickson's Flight Jackets
Full washing, machine washing, tumble drying, and conventional dry cleaning are not recommended for Buzz Rickson's flight jackets. The garment combines multiple materials and construction layers, including the nylon shell, cotton lining, pile insulation, wool knit components, leather zipper pull, elasticized sections, and metal hardware.

Exposure to water, detergent, mechanical agitation, heat, or unsuitable cleaning solvents may cause different components to react at different rates. Possible changes include dimensional distortion, shrinkage, loss of loft, deformation of the insulated body or sleeves, changes to the knitted components, puckering, uneven surface appearance, or alteration of the jacket's overall silhouette.

The fabrics and construction are intentionally developed to reproduce the character of period military garments rather than to provide the dimensional stability of modern easy-care outerwear. For this reason, aggressive cleaning may significantly alter the shape, texture, and appearance that are integral to the design of the jacket.

If localized soiling occurs, spot cleaning may be considered instead of cleaning the entire garment. A small amount of neutral detergent may be diluted with water and applied carefully with a clean cloth to the affected area. Do not saturate the fabric unnecessarily.

Even spot cleaning may cause a localized difference in color, sheen, texture, or surface appearance. Before treating a visible area, test the cleaning method on a small, inconspicuous section of the garment and allow it to dry completely before proceeding.

For significant stains, widespread soiling, or any situation in which the appropriate treatment is uncertain, we recommend consulting a professional cleaner before attempting to clean the garment yourself.

TOYS McCOY Men's Steve McQueen-Inspired Extra Heavyweight Raglan Pullover Hoodie, 14.8 oz Cotton Brushed-Back Fleece Hooded Sweatshirt, Tubular Body, Made in Japan TMC2542

TOYS McCOY

See available colors here.

This men's pullover hooded sweatshirt is made in Japan by TOYS McCOY and is inspired by the pullover hoodie worn by Steve McQueen in an off-duty photograph. Reinterpreted as a tribute to McQueen, it is made from 14.8 oz extra-heavyweight 100% cotton brushed-back sweatshirt fabric and incorporates a tubular side-seam-free body, raglan sleeves, a double-layer hood, a front kangaroo pocket, and extended rib-knit cuffs and waistband. Major joining areas, including the hood, shoulders, armholes, sleeves, cuffs, and waistband, are reinforced with parallel two-needle stitching. Together, these details create a substantial, classic athletic-sweatshirt character with a clean, understated appearance, while the relatively short body length and balanced regular fit make it easy to wear either on its own or layered under a jacket or coat.

Size and Fit Guide:

Gender: Men.

This hoodie has a balanced regular fit that is neither tight nor loose. The body is not cut excessively slim, nor does it have the exaggerated volume of an intentionally oversized silhouette. Instead, it provides moderate room through the body while keeping the overall length relatively short, creating a classic, compact shape. The raglan sleeve construction eliminates conventional shoulder seams, with the sleeves extending diagonally from the neckline to the underarms so they conform naturally around the shoulders. A relatively deep rib-knit waistband gently draws in the lower body around the waist, allowing the sweatshirt fabric to blouse slightly above the ribbing and create the softly rounded silhouette characteristic of classic sweat hoodies. The cuffs also use extended rib knit, which fits comfortably around the wrists and keeps the sleeve ends neatly in place. This balanced construction makes the hoodie easy to wear as a standalone sweatshirt while also allowing it to layer comfortably under jackets and coats.

Because fit may vary depending on body type and personal preference, please use the actual garment measurements below as your primary reference. For the most accurate comparison, we recommend measuring a similar hooded sweatshirt that fits you well. All measurements are taken by hand with a measuring tape, so slight variations may occur between individual garments and depending on the measuring method.

1958 Steve McQueen Off-Screen Design Source
In 1958, Steve McQueen was photographed relaxing at his Laurel Canyon home, where he lived with his wife, Neile Adams. In the photograph, he wore a plain pullover sweatshirt hoodie with white jeans, creating a simple off-screen combination distinct from the costumes associated with his film roles.

This TOYS McCOY model takes that private moment and McQueen's understated pullover hoodie as its design source. Rather than relying on printed graphics or conspicuous decoration, the design is defined by the structure of the sweatshirt itself, including the extra-heavyweight cotton fabric, tubular body, raglan sleeves, double-layer hood, extended rib-knit components, kangaroo pocket, and visible double-needle stitching.

These elements reinterpret the atmosphere of McQueen's off-screen sweatshirt through TOYS McCOY's approach to vintage-inspired construction, producing a current pullover hoodie based on the proportions and functional details of classic American sweatwear.

14.8-Ounce Extra-Heavyweight 100% Cotton Sweatshirt Fabric
The sweatshirt is made from 14.8-ounce extra-heavyweight fabric knitted from 100% cotton. The material has substantial thickness, physical weight, and body, giving the garment a markedly heavier and more structured character than a lightweight or medium-weight sweatshirt.

The outer surface retains the rugged character of the yarns, with clearly visible vertical columns of knitted stitches. These vertically aligned columns, technically referred to as wales, are formed by successive knitted loops running along the length of the fabric. The wales remain visible across the surface and give the fabric an identifiable knitted structure rather than the flatter appearance of a woven textile.

The yarns and knitted loops also produce subtle natural variations in height, spacing, and surface texture. The fabric therefore does not appear completely smooth or mechanically uniform. Its slight irregularity and restrained surface variation create the straightforward, rugged appearance associated with traditional American sweatshirt fabrics.

The fabric has a firm body and a distinctly dry hand rather than an exceptionally soft, fluid, or loosely draped feel. Its substantial mass can also be felt when the garment is lifted or held in the hand. Together, the dry texture, firm resilience, visible knitted structure, and physical weight give the sweatshirt the substantial character expected from an extra-heavyweight fabric.

Brushed-Back Interior
The reverse side of the sweatshirt fabric is brushed to raise the cotton fibers and form a soft, finely napped interior surface. This differs from an unbrushed loopback sweatshirt fabric, where the looped yarn structure remains visibly exposed on the reverse side.

During brushing, fibers are lifted from the reverse surface without changing the fundamental knitted construction of the fabric. The resulting nap produces a softer interior texture while adding visible and tactile volume to the already substantial 14.8-ounce material.

Small spaces form among the raised fibers, allowing the brushed layer to hold pockets of air. When combined with the thickness and density of the extra-heavyweight sweatshirt fabric, this structure helps retain warmth generated by the body.

Tubular Side-Seam-Free Body
The torso is knitted as a continuous tube on a circular knitting machine, creating what is commonly referred to as a tubular body. Unlike conventional cut-and-sewn construction, the body is not assembled from separate front and back panels joined along the left and right sides.

Because the torso forms one continuous knitted section, there are no vertical side seams along either side of the body. The corresponding seam allowances, folded edges, and overlapping layers of fabric that would normally occur at these locations are also eliminated.

Removing these side seams helps prevent localized thickness, hardness, and raised ridges from forming along the sides of the torso. This is particularly relevant with an extra-heavyweight fabric, where conventional stacked seam allowances could otherwise produce noticeable bulk. The uninterrupted tubular construction also gives the sweatshirt a clean side profile without visible vertical seam lines.

Tubular body construction is a traditional method found on vintage American T-shirts and sweatshirts. On this model, it forms an integral part of the garment's classic athletic-wear construction rather than serving as an applied decorative feature.

Unwashed Finish and Shrinkage Characteristics
The completed sweatshirt is supplied in an unwashed condition and has not undergone a final washing treatment during production. In its new state, the cotton fibers and knitted loops have not yet contracted and settled through exposure to water and drying. As a result, the spaces between the knitted loops may initially appear slightly more open.

During laundering, the cotton fibers absorb water and the knitted structure contracts naturally. As the garment dries, the loops settle closer together and the spacing between them becomes slightly tighter. This process can give the fabric a denser, more compact appearance and a firmer, more cohesive hand than it has in its original unwashed condition.

When the sweatshirt is gently hand washed in cold water, reshaped, and allowed to dry naturally in the shade, the resulting shrinkage tends to remain comparatively slight. Dimensional change is more likely to appear in the vertical direction, particularly in the body length, while the change across the body width tends to be smaller.

The exact amount and direction of shrinkage cannot be guaranteed. Results may vary according to the individual garment, water temperature, washing duration, mechanical agitation, spin intensity, reshaping after washing, and drying conditions.

Warm or hot water and tumble drying can cause the cotton fibers and knitted structure to contract more extensively. These methods may produce greater and less predictable dimensional changes and should therefore be avoided.

Raglan Sleeve Construction
The sweatshirt uses raglan sleeves. Diagonal seams extend from the area near the neckline toward the underarms, joining each sleeve directly to the body.

This differs from set-in sleeve construction, where a shaped sleeve cap is attached to an armhole at the outer end of a defined shoulder seam. The raglan configuration eliminates a conventional shoulder seam positioned at a fixed shoulder point and creates a continuous transition from the neckline across the shoulder and into the upper arm.

Because the shoulder shape is not divided by a fixed horizontal shoulder seam, the sleeve and upper-body area can settle more naturally along the individual contours of the wearer's shoulders.

Double-Layer Hood Made from Matching Sweatshirt Fabric
The hood is constructed from two layers of the same sweatshirt fabric used for the body rather than as a single-layer component. Using the extra-heavyweight fabric on both the exterior and interior gives the hood substantial thickness, physical weight, and volume.

The double-layer structure supports the three-dimensional shape of the hood and helps prevent it from collapsing completely. When the hood is not worn over the head and rests against the upper back, it retains a fuller and more clearly defined outline than a lightweight single-layer hood.

Overlapping Hood Front with Buttonhole-Style Drawcord Openings
The front edges of the hood are not simply aligned edge to edge. Instead, one side overlaps the other at the front, creating a layered construction where the two sides meet near the neckline.

A pair of buttonhole-style openings is worked into the front of the hood to provide exit points for the drawcord. A flat drawcord passes through the hood channel and emerges through these two openings, allowing the circumference of the hood opening to be adjusted.

Because the hood front uses an overlapping construction, the two drawcord exit points may appear slightly asymmetrical when the garment is worn or viewed from the front. This visual difference results from the layered position of the hood edges and is a characteristic of the construction rather than a requirement for the openings to appear perfectly symmetrical.

Kangaroo Handwarmer Pocket
A kangaroo pocket made from the same sweatshirt fabric as the body is attached to the lower front. The pocket is constructed as a separate fabric panel laid over and sewn onto the exterior surface of the sweatshirt.

Openings on the left and right lead into one continuous interior compartment. Because the two sides are internally connected rather than divided into separate pockets, either hand can pass into the same central space from either opening.

The pocket is configured primarily as a handwarmer rather than as secure storage for small objects. Its large side openings provide easy access for both hands, but the continuous interior does not prevent stored items from moving toward and falling through either opening. Small valuables should therefore not be considered securely contained within the pocket.

Extended Double-Layer Rib-Knit Sleeve Cuffs
Each sleeve is finished with a separate rib-knit cuff. The rib-knit component is folded back on itself to form a double-layer structure and is then sewn to the end of the sweatshirt sleeve.

The rib knit has greater elasticity than the main sweatshirt fabric. This allows the cuff to follow the wrist with moderate tension while accommodating normal movement of the hand and arm. Its elasticity also helps prevent the sleeve opening from spreading excessively during wear.

The cuffs are proportionally longer than those used on many standard sweatshirts and cover a broader area around the wrists. This extended construction reduces open space at the sleeve ends through which cold air can enter while creating the distinctive long-cuff proportions associated with vintage-inspired athletic sweatwear.

Extended Rib-Knit Waistband
The lower body is finished with a separate extended rib-knit waistband. Like the sleeve cuffs, the waistband has greater elasticity than the extra-heavyweight sweatshirt fabric used for the body.

The rib knit follows the waist area with moderate tension and helps the lower edge of the sweatshirt settle around the waist rather than hanging freely below it. As the lower body is drawn inward by the waistband, a small amount of the substantial sweatshirt fabric gathers naturally above the ribbing.

This relationship between the full-bodied sweatshirt fabric and the more elastic waistband creates the softly rounded, cohesive silhouette associated with classic sweatshirt construction. The extended vertical depth of the ribbing also gives the lower body the longer waistband proportions characteristic of vintage-inspired athletic sweatwear.

Double-Needle Stitching at Major Component Junctions
Double-needle stitching is used at major junctions throughout the sweatshirt, including the hood, raglan shoulder areas, armholes, sleeves, cuff attachments, and waistband attachment. Two parallel rows of stitching secure the joined components at these structural locations.

Using two rows of stitching broadens the secured area compared with a single stitched row. It also distributes tension across two parallel rows where the garment is repeatedly subjected to movement and pulling, helping stabilize the joined sections during normal wear.

The parallel rows remain visible on the exterior and make the functional seam construction part of the sweatshirt's appearance. Rather than serving as a separate decorative application, the visible stitching follows the actual component junctions and contributes to the straightforward sewing character associated with classic American sweatwear.

Decorative Label at the Front Left Hem
A decorative label is sewn onto the exterior of the front body near the left hem. Its localized placement creates a subtle visual focal point within the otherwise plain design, adding a restrained accent while preserving the clean overall appearance of the garment.

Care Instructions
Hand wash only. Do not machine wash.
Do not bleach.
Iron at a low temperature using a pressing cloth.
Do not dry clean.
Do not use a machine spin cycle. Drip dry in the shade.
Do not tumble dry.

Because this garment is made from unwashed 100% cotton sweatshirt fabric, washing allows the cotton fibers and knitted structure to contract naturally. When gently hand washed in cold water, reshaped, and dried naturally in the shade, dimensional change tends to remain comparatively limited and may be more noticeable in the body-length direction than across the body. The actual degree and direction of shrinkage can vary according to water temperature, handling, drying conditions, and individual garment characteristics. Machine washing, warm or hot water, machine spin extraction, and tumble drying may cause greater and less predictable shrinkage and should be avoided.

Always follow the care instructions attached to the actual product.

1958 Steve McQueen Off-Screen Design Source
In 1958, Steve McQueen was photographed relaxing at his Laurel Canyon home, where he lived with his wife, Neile Adams. In the photograph, he wore a plain pullover sweatshirt hoodie with white jeans, creating a simple off-screen combination distinct from the costumes associated with his film roles.

This TOYS McCOY model takes that private moment and McQueen's understated pullover hoodie as its design source. Rather than relying on printed graphics or conspicuous decoration, the design is defined by the structure of the sweatshirt itself, including the extra-heavyweight cotton fabric, tubular body, raglan sleeves, double-layer hood, extended rib-knit components, kangaroo pocket, and visible double-needle stitching.

These elements reinterpret the atmosphere of McQueen's off-screen sweatshirt through TOYS McCOY's approach to vintage-inspired construction, producing a current pullover hoodie based on the proportions and functional details of classic American sweatwear.

14.8-Ounce Extra-Heavyweight 100% Cotton Sweatshirt Fabric
The sweatshirt is made from 14.8-ounce extra-heavyweight fabric knitted from 100% cotton. The material has substantial thickness, physical weight, and body, giving the garment a markedly heavier and more structured character than a lightweight or medium-weight sweatshirt.

The outer surface retains the rugged character of the yarns, with clearly visible vertical columns of knitted stitches. These vertically aligned columns, technically referred to as wales, are formed by successive knitted loops running along the length of the fabric. The wales remain visible across the surface and give the fabric an identifiable knitted structure rather than the flatter appearance of a woven textile.

The yarns and knitted loops also produce subtle natural variations in height, spacing, and surface texture. The fabric therefore does not appear completely smooth or mechanically uniform. Its slight irregularity and restrained surface variation create the straightforward, rugged appearance associated with traditional American sweatshirt fabrics.

The fabric has a firm body and a distinctly dry hand rather than an exceptionally soft, fluid, or loosely draped feel. Its substantial mass can also be felt when the garment is lifted or held in the hand. Together, the dry texture, firm resilience, visible knitted structure, and physical weight give the sweatshirt the substantial character expected from an extra-heavyweight fabric.

Brushed-Back Interior
The reverse side of the sweatshirt fabric is brushed to raise the cotton fibers and form a soft, finely napped interior surface. This differs from an unbrushed loopback sweatshirt fabric, where the looped yarn structure remains visibly exposed on the reverse side.

During brushing, fibers are lifted from the reverse surface without changing the fundamental knitted construction of the fabric. The resulting nap produces a softer interior texture while adding visible and tactile volume to the already substantial 14.8-ounce material.

Small spaces form among the raised fibers, allowing the brushed layer to hold pockets of air. When combined with the thickness and density of the extra-heavyweight sweatshirt fabric, this structure helps retain warmth generated by the body.

Tubular Side-Seam-Free Body
The torso is knitted as a continuous tube on a circular knitting machine, creating what is commonly referred to as a tubular body. Unlike conventional cut-and-sewn construction, the body is not assembled from separate front and back panels joined along the left and right sides.

Because the torso forms one continuous knitted section, there are no vertical side seams along either side of the body. The corresponding seam allowances, folded edges, and overlapping layers of fabric that would normally occur at these locations are also eliminated.

Removing these side seams helps prevent localized thickness, hardness, and raised ridges from forming along the sides of the torso. This is particularly relevant with an extra-heavyweight fabric, where conventional stacked seam allowances could otherwise produce noticeable bulk. The uninterrupted tubular construction also gives the sweatshirt a clean side profile without visible vertical seam lines.

Tubular body construction is a traditional method found on vintage American T-shirts and sweatshirts. On this model, it forms an integral part of the garment's classic athletic-wear construction rather than serving as an applied decorative feature.

Unwashed Finish and Shrinkage Characteristics
The completed sweatshirt is supplied in an unwashed condition and has not undergone a final washing treatment during production. In its new state, the cotton fibers and knitted loops have not yet contracted and settled through exposure to water and drying. As a result, the spaces between the knitted loops may initially appear slightly more open.

During laundering, the cotton fibers absorb water and the knitted structure contracts naturally. As the garment dries, the loops settle closer together and the spacing between them becomes slightly tighter. This process can give the fabric a denser, more compact appearance and a firmer, more cohesive hand than it has in its original unwashed condition.

When the sweatshirt is gently hand washed in cold water, reshaped, and allowed to dry naturally in the shade, the resulting shrinkage tends to remain comparatively slight. Dimensional change is more likely to appear in the vertical direction, particularly in the body length, while the change across the body width tends to be smaller.

The exact amount and direction of shrinkage cannot be guaranteed. Results may vary according to the individual garment, water temperature, washing duration, mechanical agitation, spin intensity, reshaping after washing, and drying conditions.

Warm or hot water and tumble drying can cause the cotton fibers and knitted structure to contract more extensively. These methods may produce greater and less predictable dimensional changes and should therefore be avoided.

Raglan Sleeve Construction
The sweatshirt uses raglan sleeves. Diagonal seams extend from the area near the neckline toward the underarms, joining each sleeve directly to the body.

This differs from set-in sleeve construction, where a shaped sleeve cap is attached to an armhole at the outer end of a defined shoulder seam. The raglan configuration eliminates a conventional shoulder seam positioned at a fixed shoulder point and creates a continuous transition from the neckline across the shoulder and into the upper arm.

Because the shoulder shape is not divided by a fixed horizontal shoulder seam, the sleeve and upper-body area can settle more naturally along the individual contours of the wearer's shoulders.

Double-Layer Hood Made from Matching Sweatshirt Fabric
The hood is constructed from two layers of the same sweatshirt fabric used for the body rather than as a single-layer component. Using the extra-heavyweight fabric on both the exterior and interior gives the hood substantial thickness, physical weight, and volume.

The double-layer structure supports the three-dimensional shape of the hood and helps prevent it from collapsing completely. When the hood is not worn over the head and rests against the upper back, it retains a fuller and more clearly defined outline than a lightweight single-layer hood.

Overlapping Hood Front with Buttonhole-Style Drawcord Openings
The front edges of the hood are not simply aligned edge to edge. Instead, one side overlaps the other at the front, creating a layered construction where the two sides meet near the neckline.

A pair of buttonhole-style openings is worked into the front of the hood to provide exit points for the drawcord. A flat drawcord passes through the hood channel and emerges through these two openings, allowing the circumference of the hood opening to be adjusted.

Because the hood front uses an overlapping construction, the two drawcord exit points may appear slightly asymmetrical when the garment is worn or viewed from the front. This visual difference results from the layered position of the hood edges and is a characteristic of the construction rather than a requirement for the openings to appear perfectly symmetrical.

Kangaroo Handwarmer Pocket
A kangaroo pocket made from the same sweatshirt fabric as the body is attached to the lower front. The pocket is constructed as a separate fabric panel laid over and sewn onto the exterior surface of the sweatshirt.

Openings on the left and right lead into one continuous interior compartment. Because the two sides are internally connected rather than divided into separate pockets, either hand can pass into the same central space from either opening.

The pocket is configured primarily as a handwarmer rather than as secure storage for small objects. Its large side openings provide easy access for both hands, but the continuous interior does not prevent stored items from moving toward and falling through either opening. Small valuables should therefore not be considered securely contained within the pocket.

Extended Double-Layer Rib-Knit Sleeve Cuffs
Each sleeve is finished with a separate rib-knit cuff. The rib-knit component is folded back on itself to form a double-layer structure and is then sewn to the end of the sweatshirt sleeve.

The rib knit has greater elasticity than the main sweatshirt fabric. This allows the cuff to follow the wrist with moderate tension while accommodating normal movement of the hand and arm. Its elasticity also helps prevent the sleeve opening from spreading excessively during wear.

The cuffs are proportionally longer than those used on many standard sweatshirts and cover a broader area around the wrists. This extended construction reduces open space at the sleeve ends through which cold air can enter while creating the distinctive long-cuff proportions associated with vintage-inspired athletic sweatwear.

Extended Rib-Knit Waistband
The lower body is finished with a separate extended rib-knit waistband. Like the sleeve cuffs, the waistband has greater elasticity than the extra-heavyweight sweatshirt fabric used for the body.

The rib knit follows the waist area with moderate tension and helps the lower edge of the sweatshirt settle around the waist rather than hanging freely below it. As the lower body is drawn inward by the waistband, a small amount of the substantial sweatshirt fabric gathers naturally above the ribbing.

This relationship between the full-bodied sweatshirt fabric and the more elastic waistband creates the softly rounded, cohesive silhouette associated with classic sweatshirt construction. The extended vertical depth of the ribbing also gives the lower body the longer waistband proportions characteristic of vintage-inspired athletic sweatwear.

Double-Needle Stitching at Major Component Junctions
Double-needle stitching is used at major junctions throughout the sweatshirt, including the hood, raglan shoulder areas, armholes, sleeves, cuff attachments, and waistband attachment. Two parallel rows of stitching secure the joined components at these structural locations.

Using two rows of stitching broadens the secured area compared with a single stitched row. It also distributes tension across two parallel rows where the garment is repeatedly subjected to movement and pulling, helping stabilize the joined sections during normal wear.

The parallel rows remain visible on the exterior and make the functional seam construction part of the sweatshirt's appearance. Rather than serving as a separate decorative application, the visible stitching follows the actual component junctions and contributes to the straightforward sewing character associated with classic American sweatwear.

Decorative Label at the Front Left Hem
A decorative label is sewn onto the exterior of the front body near the left hem. Its localized placement creates a subtle visual focal point within the otherwise plain design, adding a restrained accent while preserving the clean overall appearance of the garment.

Care Instructions
Hand wash only. Do not machine wash.
Do not bleach.
Iron at a low temperature using a pressing cloth.
Do not dry clean.
Do not use a machine spin cycle. Drip dry in the shade.
Do not tumble dry.

Because this garment is made from unwashed 100% cotton sweatshirt fabric, washing allows the cotton fibers and knitted structure to contract naturally. When gently hand washed in cold water, reshaped, and dried naturally in the shade, dimensional change tends to remain comparatively limited and may be more noticeable in the body-length direction than across the body. The actual degree and direction of shrinkage can vary according to water temperature, handling, drying conditions, and individual garment characteristics. Machine washing, warm or hot water, machine spin extraction, and tumble drying may cause greater and less predictable shrinkage and should be avoided.

Always follow the care instructions attached to the actual product.

Buzz Rickson's Men's Off-White Chambray Long-Sleeve Work Shirt, Modified 1950s U.S. Navy Utility Shirt Design, Made in Japan (BR25996 105 Ecru-Toned Off-White)

Buzz Rickson

This men's long-sleeve button-up shirt is made in Japan by Buzz Rickson's, Toyo Enterprise's military label specializing in vintage-inspired American military clothing. Its construction is based on the blue chambray utility shirts worn by U.S. Navy sailors during the 1950s, but the original blue chambray has been replaced with an ecru-toned off-white chambray, creating a distinctive Buzz Rickson's reinterpretation rather than an exact color reproduction. The lightweight 100% cotton chambray displays natural weave irregularities, small neps, and subtle, linen-like wrinkling, giving the fabric a rough, rustic workwear character. The shirt incorporates period-inspired details such as a collar stand, flapless buttoned chest pockets, rounded shirttail hem, selvedge side gussets, and chain-stitch runoffs extending from the side seams at the hem. Together, these details preserve the practical character of the original design while giving the shirt a lighter, more understated appearance. Its balanced silhouette is neither overly slim nor excessively loose, allowing it to blend naturally into contemporary casual wardrobes.

Size and Fit Guide:

The shoulders and body are not cut especially narrow, nor does the shirt have the added volume of an intentionally oversized design. The front and back are finished with a gently rounded shirttail hem, making the shirt suitable for wearing either tucked in or untucked.
